newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel urges okay of SmithKline's carvedilol.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel urges okay of SmithKline's carvedilol.

text.p: A Food and Drug Administration advisory committee voted 8-2 Thursday to recommend approval of SmithKline Beecham's carvedilol (COREG) for congestive heart failure (CHF).
The FDA does not have to follow the panel's advice, but usually does.
In CHF the heart weakens and loses its ability to pump blood eventually leading to death. Three to four million Americans currently have the condition.
Carvedilol, a beta blocker, was reviewed by the same panel in May 1996, but it did not recommend approval, saying there was not enough evidence of its efficacy.
At that meeting, Smithkline presented data from eight trials, several of which were terminated early so that people taking a placebo could be switched to carvedilol.

On Thursday, Smithkline re-analyzed data from three of those trials and presented new data from a study done in Australia and New Zealand. That study showed that carvedilol improved the heart's pumping ability by 5.3 percent but did not improve patients' ability to tolerate exercise.
Results were published in the February 7 issue of the London medical journal the Lancet.
Neil Shusterman, vice president of clinical research at Smithkline, told the panel that in that trial, carvedilol reduced the risk of morbidity and mortality by 23 percent.
The figure is not as impressive as recorded by earlier trials.
Also, the panel questioned the firm's methods of calculating the risk.

Despite the panel's doubts about the true rate of reduction, members said that based on all the evidence, carvedilol seemed to be effective at easing CHF symptoms and had some impact on morbidity and mortality.

"I don't have difficulty in believing that carvedilol is a good drug for CHF, but it may need to be labeled (for proper usage)," said panel member Michael Weber, of the Brookville University Hospital Medical Center in Brooklyn.
